emergency.notes: 999 or 112 — both work for all services.

healthcare.costForTourists: Emergency treatment at A&E (ER) is free for everyone. Non-emergency GP visits and prescriptions are charged to non-UK residents. Walk-in centres handle minor issues. Private clinics £80-150 for consultation.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Boots and Lloyds pharmacies everywhere. Pharmacists can provide advice and sell many OTC medications. Some medications that require prescriptions in the US are OTC in the UK (e.g., stronger pain relief).
healthcare.hospitalNotes: NHS hospitals provide good emergency care. Wait times can be long for non-emergencies. Private hospitals (Bupa, HCA) offer faster service but are expensive. London has excellent specialist hospitals.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Emergency A&E is free. Travel insurance recommended for non-emergency care, dental, and repatriation.

controlledSubstances.note: Low-dose codeine (co-codamol, Nurofen Plus) available OTC at pharmacies.
CBD products legal if they contain less than 0.2% THC. Available in health food shops.

medications.generalAdvice: The UK is relatively relaxed on medications. Bring prescriptions for controlled substances. Many common medications available OTC at pharmacies that would require prescriptions in the US.

scams.name: Card skimming at tourist ATMs
scams.description: ATMs near tourist sites may have skimming devices. Also, currency conversion ATMs offer poor exchange rates.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks. Always choose to be charged in local currency (GBP), not USD.

scams.name: Fake ticket sellers
scams.description: Touts outside West End theatres and sporting events sell fake or overpriced tickets.
scams.avoidance: Only buy from official box offices or authorized resellers (TKTS booth in Leicester Square for discounted theatre tickets).

scams.name: Unlicensed minicabs
scams.description: Unlicensed cars offer rides outside clubs and bars late at night. Safety risk — some involve robbery.
scams.avoidance: Only use black cabs (can be hailed) or pre-booked minicabs via apps (Uber, Bolt, Free Now). Licensed minicabs cannot be hailed on the street.

connectivity.simOptions: Three, EE, or Vodafone SIM at airports and high-street shops. £10-15 for 30 days. eSIM via Airalo. Three and EE have excellent UK coverage.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi widely available — cafes, pubs, restaurants, trains, the Tube (in stations). Very reliable.
connectivity.bestOption: Three SIM (great value, includes roaming in 71 countries) or eSIM.

cultural.tipping: 10-12.5% at restaurants if service charge not included (check the bill). £1 per drink at bars is generous. Black cab drivers: round up. Not expected at pubs or for counter service.
cultural.dressCode: Casual but Brits dress smartly for dinner, theatre, and pubs on weekends. No dress code for most venues. Smart casual covers most situations.
cultural.greetings: Handshake for first meetings. Friends may hug. 'Alright?' is a greeting, not a question — respond with 'Alright' or 'Good, thanks.'
taboos: Being overly loud or enthusiastic (keep volume down)
Confusing England with Britain, or Scotland with England
cultural.haggling: Not practiced. Only at car boot sales and some markets.

safety.lgbtSafety: Same-sex marriage legal. Very tolerant. London has one of the world's largest LGBTQ+ communities (Soho). Other major cities are welcoming.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally safe. Normal urban precautions at night. Well-lit, well-policed city centers.
safety.notes: The UK is safe for tourists. Pickpocketing in London tourist areas and late-night antisocial behavior in city centers after pubs close are the main concerns. Knife crime exists but rarely affects tourist areas.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 6 months visa-free. EU citizens: pre-settled/settled status or ETA required post-Brexit.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: May-September for best weather. June-August warmest. December for Christmas markets. Rain is possible year-round — bring layers.
